title: Pointers & Arrays: The Moving Cursor
description: Work through addresses, dereferencing, pointer arithmetic, and what an array can do that a lone pointer cannot.
congratsText: You can now aim a cursor at an array, slide it, write through it, and say exactly where a lone pointer falls short.
objectives: Explain what an address is and what a pointer variable actually stores
Distinguish reading a value with * from re-aiming the pointer itself
Identify an array's name as the address of its first item
Predict what happens when a value is stored where an address belongs
Calculate where cursor + n lands in an array of ints
Apply a cursor walk that reaches every item without an index
Compare the three equivalent forms arr[i], *(arr + i), and *(p + i)
Contrast what sizeof and assignment do to an array name versus a pointer
Evaluate why stepping past the end is unsafe even when nothing crashes
recap: Every variable sits at an address; & gets it and a pointer variable stores it
*cursor reads or writes the value; plain cursor holds the location
An array's name is already the address of its first item, so no & is needed
Storing a plain number in a pointer compiles with a warning and leaves junk behind
cursor + 1 jumps one whole int, not one byte
Reading then sliding the cursor each pass walks the array with no index
arr[i] is shorthand the compiler rewrites as *(arr + i)
sizeof sees a whole array but only one address of a pointer, and an array name cannot be reassigned
C never checks bounds, so keeping the loop inside the array is your job

sections.title: Addresses & the Pointer That Holds One

chunks.text: Every variable sits somewhere in memory, and that spot has a numeric address. The & operator hands you that address.

check.question: What does &total give you?

chunks.text: Print an address with the %p specifier. %d is for the value, not for the location.

check.question: Which specifier prints an address?

chunks.text: A pointer is a variable built to hold an address: int *cursor = &total; stores where total lives, not what it holds.

check.question: Is int *cursor = total; a valid way to aim a cursor?

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: Nothing, cursor was never given a value

sections.title: Reading and Writing Through the Star

chunks.text: *cursor means go to that address and look inside, so it gives you a value. Plain cursor gives you the location.

check.question: Which one prints a value?

chunks.text: The star also works on the left of =. Writing *cursor = 99; drops 99 into the box the cursor is parked on.

check.question: *cursor = 99; changes what?

chunks.text: Drop the star and the meaning flips. cursor = 99; tries to re-aim the cursor at address 99 instead of storing 99 anywhere.

check.question: cursor = 99; stores 99 in the box the cursor was on.

sections.title: The Array Name Is Already an Address

chunks.text: An array's name is the address of its first item, which is why prices and &prices[0] print the same address.

check.question: prices and &prices[0] are what?

chunks.text: So a pointer can be aimed at an array with no & at all. cursor = prices; is enough, because the name is already an address.

check.question: Do you need & when writing cursor = prices;?

chunks.text: Once aimed, *cursor and prices[0] are two labels on one box, so reading either gives the same number.

check.question: *cursor and prices[0] read from what?

chunks.text: C will often let a suspicious line through with only a warning, which means the program still builds and still runs.

check.question: A warning always stops the build.

chunks.text: Storing a plain number in a pointer is one of those lines. It compiles with a complaint, and the pointer is left holding a nonsense address.

check.question: int *p = 100; produces what?

chunks.text: Reading through a nonsense address is undefined behavior. It might print garbage on your machine and crash on the one beside you.

check.question: Same bad pointer, same result every run?

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a line that stores the address of score in a pointer named p.

chunks.text: cursor + 1 does not add one byte. It moves forward by one whole item, which is 4 bytes for an int.

check.question: cursor + 1 moves forward by what?

chunks.text: That makes *(cursor + 1) the next item and *(cursor + 3) the fourth one, counting from where the cursor is parked.

check.question: With the cursor at the start, *(cursor + 2) reads which slot?

chunks.text: cursor++ makes the same jump, but it also leaves the cursor there. The pointer itself has moved.

check.question: cursor++ leaves the cursor where it was.

sections.title: Walking the Shelf Without an Index

chunks.text: A loop can read where the cursor sits, then slide it one step. Repeat that and you touch every item without ever writing prices[i].

check.question: Can you walk an array using no index at all?

chunks.text: Order inside the body matters. Read first with printf("%d", *cursor); and slide after with cursor++;.

check.question: Swapping those two lines would do what?

chunks.text: In a cursor walk the counter i is only counting passes. It never picks the slot, and the cursor keeps its own position.

check.question: In a cursor walk, i picks the slot being read.

quiz.question: Arrange these into a cursor walk: the setup line first, then the two lines inside the loop body in the order they must run.

sections.title: Three Ways to Name the Same Item

chunks.text: With the cursor parked at the start, prices[i], *(prices + i), and *(cursor + i) all land on the same item.

check.question: Do all three forms give the same value there?

chunks.text: That is not a coincidence. The compiler rewrites prices[i] as *(prices + i), so brackets are shorthand for pointer math.

check.question: Brackets are shorthand for pointer math.

chunks.text: The match only holds while the cursor is still at the start. Slide it, and *(cursor + i) lines up somewhere else entirely.

check.question: After one cursor++, *(cursor + 1) is the same as what?

quiz.question: What does this print?

chunks.text: sizeof(prices) reports the whole shelf, 5 ints at 4 bytes each. sizeof(cursor) reports one address, usually 8 bytes.

check.question: sizeof on a pointer measures the whole array.

chunks.text: A pointer can be re-aimed any time, but an array name cannot be reassigned. prices = cursor; is refused outright.

check.question: prices = cursor; gives you what?

chunks.text: That is the trade. The array knows its own length and stays put, while the pointer roams freely and knows nothing about size.

check.question: Which one knows how long the row is?

quiz.question: Type the number this prints where an int is 4 bytes.

chunks.text: A five-item shelf has slots 0 through 4. Slide the cursor once more and it is parked on a slot you never filled.

check.question: A 5-item array has a slot numbered 5.

chunks.text: C never checks bounds for you. The read simply succeeds, printing whatever byte happened to be sitting at that spot.

check.question: Does C stop an out-of-bounds read?

chunks.text: Once an array is only a pointer, sizeof can no longer tell you the length. Carrying the size yourself is the only way to stop on time.

check.question: Who has to stop the walk in time?

quiz.question: What is the most likely result?
